title: Women scholars today
hook: women teaching fiqh, hadith and Qur'an across the world

segments.voice: Yesterday: scholarship today, from Cairo, Najaf and Qom to Deoband, Medina and a laptop. Your line was where they study. Today, who teaches.

A group of women in Medina has a complaint, and they bring it straight to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The men, they say, are always around you. They get all your time. So give us a day of our own. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. He agrees. He promises them a day, meets them on it, and teaches them. No one in the report tells them to wait for their husbands to pass the lessons on. They asked for a teacher, and they got one.
screen: `THE MEN GET ALL YOUR TIME.` → `GIVE US A DAY.` → `HE AGREES, AND TEACHES THEM.`

segments.voice: Begin with the Qur'an, which speaks to women and men side by side. In Pickthall's translation, one verse runs: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe," and it goes on, pair after pair, the truthful, the patient, the humble, the fasting, the ones who remember Allah, and promises all of them forgiveness and a reward. Then the women who asked for a day. They didn't wait for knowledge to trickle down to them. They went to the source. Tradition says the companions brought their questions to a woman too: 'Aisha, the Prophet's wife. Al-Bukhari's collection carries her reports, and in some she corrects what others had passed on, as when she answers a report about the dead and the weeping of their families. Tradition remembers women after her too, who taught hadith and law in their own cities, and whose names stand in the chains of transmission alongside men's. One of them, Karima of Merv, is remembered for teaching Sahih al-Bukhari itself. And today? Women teach the Qur'an and its recitation, hadith, and fiqh, the law of daily life, in mosques, seminaries and colleges, in living rooms and online classes. Communities and schools of thought hold different views on how and where women should teach, and to whom, and those views are held seriously. But the line from the hook still runs: women asking for a teacher, and a Prophet who set the day.
screen: `MEN AND WOMEN, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THEY WENT TO THE SOURCE.` · `'AISHA SETS THE RECORD STRAIGHT.` · `WOMEN IN THE CHAINS, THEN AND NOW.` · then, large: `SHE TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a woman who taught you something that stuck, a mother, a grandmother, a teacher, an aunt in a kitchen, a neighbor who knew things, and picture her face as she explained it. What did she know that you didn't? Thank her in your head for a moment, and if you pray, remember her in your prayers.
Women scholars today. Women teaching Qur'an, hadith and the law of daily life, in a line that runs back to 'Aisha and the women who asked for a day. Today's word.
Your line: she teaches. And she has, from Medina all the way until now. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslim women study and teach Qur'an recitation, hadith and fiqh in mosques, seminaries, universities and online, and communities differ on the settings in which women teach.

chat.says: Were there ever women who taught Islam, or is that something new?
options: Not new. 'Aisha corrected reports, and Karima of Merv taught Sahih al-Bukhari.
New. Early on, women only learned what their husbands passed on.
Only recently, once colleges began to admit women as students.
